name: barrier-countdown-latch
intent: Coordinate a known set of concurrent participants at a phase boundary that releases everyone only after all parties arrive (a reusable barrier), or let one or more waiters observe a fixed number of independent completions (a one-shot countdown latch), with explicit timeout, cancellation and failure propagation instead of ad-hoc counters and polling.
problem: Parallel work needs either a true rendezvous - no participant may enter phase N+1 until every declared sibling finished phase N - or a fan-in gate - a collector must not publish until N producers completed. Hand-rolled counters, flags and sleep loops spin, miss wakeups and hide the hardest failure: a worker that exits, throws or is cancelled without signalling leaves an indefinite waiter, while a wrong party count releases incomplete work or never releases at all.
context: Shared-memory concurrency or a runtime-managed group of known participants - iterative parallel solvers and simulations, multi-stage batch or map-reduce pipelines, fan-out/fan-in service startup and warm-up, load-test harnesses, and distributed runtimes that expose a stage-wide barrier. Participants run in threads, tasks, processes or orchestrated execution slots; the enclosing scope can name the group, and it must define what happens when one participant never arrives (timeout, abort, broken state or cooperative cancellation).
benefits: Phase alignment without polling: participants block in the scheduler instead of spinning, so waiting costs no CPU and release is immediate once the last party arrives.

One primitive replaces the ad-hoc counter, and with it the whole class of missed-wakeup bugs: the count, the release condition and the happens-before edge between arrival and continuation live inside the barrier rather than in hand-written flags.
Reusability by construction: a cyclic barrier resets itself every generation, so a fixed party of workers loops through many phases with one object and no re-allocation.

A built-in leader slot: the barrier action, PTHREAD_BARRIER_SERIAL_THREAD or is_leader() names exactly one participant to do per-phase work (merge partials, publish state) after everyone arrived and before anyone continues.
Fan-in collapses to one continuation: a latch turns N completions into a single point a collector can wait on or chain off, with no reduction protocol and no custom accumulator.
Failure becomes explicit instead of accidental: broken-barrier results, timeouts and abort paths surface a dead or mis-counted participant as an error rather than as a silent hang.
tradeoffs: Liveness is a group property: the rendezvous releases only when the declared number of participants arrives, so one crashed, cancelled or mis-counted participant blocks everyone. The pattern is only usable together with a break/abort/timeout policy - Java models it as all-or-none BrokenBarrierException, Python as BrokenBarrierError, pthreads as undefined behaviour on a wrong count.

Lockstep stragglers: every phase costs the slowest participant, so ordinary load imbalance is amplified rather than absorbed, and adding a barrier can turn a mildly unbalanced parallel loop into a serialized one.

Contention ceiling: the rendezvous is one shared point, so arrivals serialize on a single counter and condition variable (and flush cache lines); scaling flattens well before the CPUs are busy, and very large parties need tiered structures (Phaser, hierarchical barriers) to stay cheap.

Thread-model mismatch: a blocking wait occupies a thread, so a barrier must not be awaited on an event-loop or UI thread, nor on the same bounded pool that executes the counted work - the classic pool-starvation deadlock.

Lifecycle confusion: one-shot latches cannot be reset (a fresh instance per round), while cyclic barriers auto-reset; mixing them up either allocates per iteration or silently reuses a generation that was already broken.

Party bookkeeping is a hard invariant: the count must match the actual participants, dynamic membership needs Phaser-like machinery, and a participant that retires changes the release condition for everyone.
Diagnosis cost: a stuck barrier looks like a frozen process, and without per-phase logging, timeouts and broken-state checks it is hard to tell a dead worker from a merely slow one.

participants.responsibility: The synchronization object holding the party count (or the remaining count) and the release condition; it owns the generation and broken/aborted state and the memory-visibility edge between the last arrival and every release.
Performs one phase of work, arrives at the rendezvous and blocks until released; in barrier forms it may be the designated leader for phase-local work.
In the latch form, the single caller that waits for the counted completions and continues - or aborts - when the count reaches zero; it does not perform the counted work itself.
Per-phase work executed exactly once per generation after the last arrival and before any release: partial-result reduction, state publication, phase bookkeeping.
In the latch form, each producer that signals one completion on every exit path, including the error path, so the waiter cannot be stranded by a failure.

The defined behaviour when a participant cannot arrive: timeout, abort or reset, broken-state propagation, or an explicit cancellation signal that releases every waiter instead of letting the group hang.

use_cases: Iterative parallel solvers and simulations (Jacobi/SOR, domain decomposition, lattice updates) where no worker may read the neighbour state of iteration N+1 before every worker finished iteration N.
Map-reduce style batch jobs and shard fan-in: a collector waits for all N shards - or for the last contributor - before merging and publishing results.

Service warm-up and fan-out startup: begin accepting traffic only after N caches, connection pools and feature clients report ready, with a bounded wait so a dead dependency fails startup instead of hanging it.
Parallel test and load-generation harnesses that must have all workers positioned before a timed section starts and release them together.
Multi-stage pipelines whose workers rendezvous between stages, using the barrier action to swap roles or publish the stage's output before the next stage begins.
Coordinated checkpointing in long-running workers: a latch per round so a snapshot starts only when every worker reached a safe point.

Parallel checkout optimization: coordinate multiple independent service calls (inventory, fraud, shipping, loyalty, promotions, pricing) that must all complete before rendering the checkout page, using a barrier to fan-in their results with sub-second latency budgets.

Distributed simulation synchronization: in agent-based or physics simulations, each simulation step requires all compute nodes to finish their slice before the next timestep begins, ensuring spatial/temporal consistency across the domain.

Apache Spark's barrier execution mode launches a fixed task set that must enter a stage-wide rendezvous together; use it for gang-scheduled stages, not as a replacement for ordinary Spark task fan-in.
avoid_when: The work is a plain one-shot fork/join with no phase boundary: join the tasks or threads (Promise.all/Future.all, Task.WhenAll, Future.await, thread::join, or a structured-concurrency scope) instead of introducing a shared synchronizer.

Only the number of concurrent operations must be bounded: use a counting semaphore, whose permits represent resource capacity and can be reacquired; its release does not mean that a fixed group finished or that phases align.

The runtime is asynchronous and blocking a thread is unacceptable: use Promise.all, Future.all, CompletableFuture.allOf, asyncio.gather, awaitAll, TaskGroup or the runtime's own async barrier rather than importing a blocking wait.
Participants are independent and never need to observe each other's phase: a barrier adds coupling, contention and a deadlock surface without providing a useful invariant.
The fan-in set is unbounded or streams over time: use a queue with an explicit completion signal or an operator-style aggregation that can represent unknown N.

The runtime already owns task completion and cancellation (for example Promise.all/Future.all, Task.WhenAll, TaskGroup or errgroup): compose those handles so errors propagate instead of hiding them behind a latch.

The synchronization crosses machines without a runtime-provided distributed barrier: an in-process primitive cannot coordinate remote participants; use the system's distributed coordination protocol instead.
anti_patterns: Wrong move: use the barrier as a lock -> failure: no participant is excluded and one missing party can stall the group -> instead: use a mutex for ownership or a semaphore for capacity.

Wrong move: let runtime membership drift from the declared party count -> failure: the barrier releases early or waits forever -> instead: register/deregister with Phaser or adjust membership before the generation.
Wrong move: perform long or unbounded work after arriving -> failure: one straggler serializes every phase -> instead: finish work before arriving and keep the hook bounded.
Wrong move: reuse a one-shot latch -> failure: a later await returns immediately on stale completion or cannot be re-armed -> instead: allocate a new latch per round or use a cyclic barrier.

Wrong move: await on the same bounded pool that runs counted tasks -> failure: the waiter consumes the producer slot and self-deadlocks -> instead: use a separate coordinator or non-blocking task composition.
Wrong move: implement the rendezvous with polling or unpredicated condition waits -> failure: CPU burn, missed wakeups or races -> instead: use the platform primitive with a predicate and timeout.

Wrong move: block a barrier wait in an event loop, UI thread or shared coroutine loop -> failure: producers cannot run and the group times out or freezes -> instead: use the async barrier/task combinator or move blocking work off-loop.
design_principles: Declare the rendezvous contract: the party count (or completion count) is part of the interface, and mismatches must be detected rather than absorbed.
Fail-safe liveness over perfect synchronization: every wait is bounded (timeout, cancellation, abort) so a missing participant degrades the group instead of freezing it.
Single responsibility: the barrier holds synchronization state only; business state and phase results stay with the participants or the phase hook.
Separate arrival from work: the phase hook (barrier action or leader slot) runs once per generation and keeps aggregation out of the participants' race.
Prefer the platform primitive over a hand-rolled counter; when the runtime's concurrency model cannot block, use the runtime's own construct instead of importing a blocking one.
Structured lifetime: the rendezvous lives inside the scope that owns the participants, so cancelling that scope also releases or aborts the waiters.
best_practices: Use the standard primitive rather than a shared counter: std::barrier/std::latch, CyclicBarrier/CountDownLatch/Phaser, threading.Barrier/asyncio.Barrier, Barrier/CountdownEvent, sync.WaitGroup plus errgroup, std::sync::Barrier, pthread_barrier_t, DispatchGroup/TaskGroup.
Always bind the wait: timed await or wait(timeout), a cancellation token, or an abort path, plus a caller-visible error when the rendezvous is broken.
Decide one-shot versus reusable explicitly - allocate a fresh latch per round or use a cyclic barrier; never reuse a latch by accident.
Do per-phase aggregation in the barrier action or leader slot rather than in a separate last-arrival protocol.
Keep the wait off the thread that must also produce: separate pools for producers and the collector, or use the non-blocking combinator form.
Count and name the participants in one place; adjust the party count whenever membership changes, or use a dynamic primitive (Phaser) when workers come and go.
Test the failure paths as first-class scenarios - participant skipped, participant throws, cancellation, timeout - and log phases and generations so a hang can be attributed to a participant.
Wrap the countdown or arrival signal in a finally/defer/try-finally block so that exceptional exits still release the latch/barrier rather than stranding waiters.

Prefer structured concurrency scopes (TaskGroup, scope::spawn, errgroup) over bare threads with a shared barrier: cancellation of the scope automatically tears down participants rather than leaving them at a dangling rendezvous.
Log arrival and release events with generation numbers: when a barrier hangs, generation-correlated logs immediately isolate the straggler without requiring a debugger attachment.
pitfalls: countdown-not-in-final: Wrong move: call countDown(), arrive() or Done() only after successful work -> failure: an exception or cancellation skips the signal and strands every waiter -> instead: signal in finally/defer/ensure and report the worker failure separately. [severity: critical; languages: java, python, go, cpp]

pool-starvation-deadlock: Awaiting the latch or barrier inside a bounded thread pool while producers also run on that same pool: the waiter occupies a slot the producers need, creating a self-deadlock that only manifests under load. [severity: high; languages: java, python, go]

one-shot-reuse: Reusing a CountDownLatch or latch equivalent across a second phase without recreating it: the second await returns immediately (count already zero) but the work for that phase has not actually completed, producing silent data corruption or stale results. [severity: critical; languages: java, python, cpp]

party-count-mismatch: The declared party count does not match the actual number of participants at runtime: workers added, removed, or retried without updating the count cause the barrier to either release early (incomplete work) or hang forever (over-counted). [severity: high; languages: java, python, cpp, rust]

broken-barrier-not-handled: Catching BrokenBarrierException or BrokenBarrierError and continuing instead of aborting the phase: the barrier is in a broken state and subsequent await calls will immediately throw again, leading to cascading failures that are hard to attribute. [severity: medium; languages: java, python]

interrupt-status-not-restored: Catching InterruptedException during an await and not re-interrupting the current thread: the interrupt flag is consumed, so the thread appears unaffected but downstream blocking operations will also miss the interrupt, making cancellation unreliable. [severity: medium; languages: java]

cyclic-barrier-single-party: Using a CyclicBarrier or barrier with a party count of 1: the barrier trips on every single await with no actual synchronization, and the second phase will deadlock because the same thread cannot arrive twice as two distinct parties. [severity: medium; languages: java, python, cpp]

barrier-in-event-loop: Using a blocking barrier wait (threading.Barrier, CountDownLatch.await) inside an asyncio event loop or UI thread: the loop cannot process other tasks, effectively serializing what should be concurrent work and causing timeouts or UI freeze. [severity: high; languages: python, javascript]

waitgroup-add-inside-goroutine: Calling WaitGroup.Add() from within the goroutine after it has started instead of before: this races with the Wait() call on the parent and can cause a deadlock that manifests non-deterministically. [severity: critical; languages: go]

dropped-barrier-while-waiting: Allowing the barrier object to be dropped (Python GC, C++ RAII destructor, Rust Drop) while threads are still waiting: results in undefined behavior (C++ std::terminate, Rust silent corruption, Python BrokenBarrierError). [severity: high; languages: python, cpp, rust]

await-without-timeout: Wrong move: call an indefinite await()/wait() when a participant or dependency can fail -> failure: the collector hangs forever with no failure boundary -> instead: use a timed wait or cancellation/abort path and treat timeout as group failure. [severity: high; languages: java, python, go, csharp]

latch-success-confusion: Wrong move: treat a latch reaching zero as proof that every producer succeeded -> failure: a failed worker can still signal completion and the collector publishes partial or invalid state -> instead: record errors/results separately and gate publication on both completion and success. [severity: high; languages: java, python, go, csharp]
sources: Oracle, Java SE 21 API: java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier and CountDownLatch - originating catalog citation for this row (docs/design-patterns.md footnote for Barrier / Countdown Latch).

related_patterns_notes.counting-semaphore: controls concurrent access to a limited resource; it does not wait for a fixed group to finish or align phases.
related_patterns_notes.future-promise: represents one asynchronous result and composes fan-in; use it instead of a blocking latch when results and failure propagation are already task-shaped.
related_patterns_notes.structured-concurrency: scopes child lifetimes and propagates cancellation; it usually replaces a one-shot latch but does not itself create a reusable phase rendezvous.
related_patterns_notes.fork-join: joins child tasks after their work; it is the simpler one-shot alternative when no shared phase boundary is needed.
related_patterns_notes.thread-pool: supplies execution capacity; do not confuse its worker count with the barrier party count.
related_patterns_notes.producer-consumer: decouples work through a queue; it absorbs arrival skew where a barrier intentionally couples workers.
related_patterns_notes.guarded-suspension: waits for a state predicate under a guard; it protects a resource or state condition rather than requiring all named parties.
related_patterns_notes.cancellation-token: propagates stop intent; pair it with a bounded wait to break a stuck barrier rather than treating cancellation as arrival.
related_patterns_notes.phaser: supports dynamic registration and multi-phase advance; choose it when party membership changes and a fixed CyclicBarrier count does not fit.
related_patterns_notes.staged-event-barrier: sequences asynchronous stages or events; it can replace a blocking barrier in event-driven runtimes but does not imply thread rendezvous.
related_patterns_notes.active-object: serializes requests behind an object's executor; it avoids shared-party waiting rather than aligning independent workers.
